info.title: Power Automate API
info.description:
The Power Automate service API (`api.flow.microsoft.com`), which addresses flows under the `Microsoft.ProcessSimple` resource provider -- the internal name Power Automate still carries on the wire.

It is a sibling of the Power Apps API rather than part of the Power Platform API: same shape, same `/providers/{rp}/environments/{env}/...` convention, same `scopes/admin` elevation, and its own host.

Unofficial and reverse-engineered. Every operation here was read from a shipped client's call sites rather than from documentation -- Microsoft's own PowerShell administration module, the Power Platform admin centre's JavaScript, and third-party clients -- so the routes and methods are real, and the response shapes are the ones those clients expect rather than replies anyone here has seen. See the [README](https://github.com/AdamCoulterOz/powerplatform-apis/tree/main/flow).

x-notes.note:
**This spec is client-derived and nothing in it has been observed on the wire.** It exists because the corpus was silent on Power Automate while every other Power Platform surface was covered, and a reader comparing a working client against the corpus would have found nothing at all here.

That still makes it the weakest spec in the corpus by evidence, though it is no longer the thinnest: no operation carries `x-probe-verified`; the response shapes are what clients expect, read from their own test fixtures and from the fields their code reaches for, never from a reply seen here; and each `api-version` is the one a shipped client sends rather than one the service was seen to accept. Treat it as a map of what exists and is called, not as a contract.

What has changed is the grading. Operations are no longer all `provider`: each one now carries the strongest source that witnesses it, and `x-corroborated-by` lists the weaker sources that witness the same route independently. Agreement between a Microsoft client and a third-party one is worth reading -- it is the only kind of confirmation available here -- but it is agreement about the request, never about the reply.

**The api-version on every PowerShell-derived route is a client default, not a service requirement.** Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell carries `{apiVersion}` as a macro in each route literal and fills it from the cmdlet's own default parameter, which a caller can override with `-ApiVersion`. So the defaults recorded here are what those cmdlets send; they say nothing about which versions the service accepts, and nothing about which it rejects.

The same is true of the host. The module resolves it per cloud from the signed-in session rather than hardcoding it, and the value in this spec's `servers` block is the public-cloud one.

**`scopes/admin/` is an optional path segment, and that is why some operations appear twice here.** In cli-microsoft365 it is a `--asAdmin` switch that concatenates either `scopes/admin/` or an empty string into the URL, so one call site is two concrete routes. OpenAPI has no way to describe an optional segment, so each is written out: `flows_get` and `flows_getAdmin`, `flows_start` and `flows_startAdmin`, and so on.

The axis is not uniform. `restore` and `modifyowners` exist **only** on the admin scope, the admin flow list inserts a `/v2/` segment as well as the scope, and `modifyPermissions` is called on the user scope by the same module that calls `modifyowners` on the admin one. Do not assume a route has an admin twin because its neighbour does.

**`~default` is a value, not a route.** Clients substitute the literal `~default` for the environment name to mean the tenant default environment, so it is documented as a value of `environmentName` rather than as a path of its own.

**A first-party rewrite of this surface exists, and it is not this host.** The current Power Automate maker portal does not call `api.flow.microsoft.com` at all. Its bundle authors legacy `Microsoft.ProcessSimple` URLs and rewrites them in an interceptor: strip `providers/Microsoft.ProcessSimple`, lift `environments/{id}` out of the path and into the hostname, prefix `/powerautomate`, and force `api-version=1`. The result is the `/powerautomate/` family on the environment-scoped Power Platform API host, documented in spec:ppapi. The rewrite is gated by `isPPAPIFlowEnabled`, which is hard-coded true in the shipped settings, so for that client the routes in THIS spec are dead code.

This spec is still the right description for everyone else: the Power Platform CLI, the `Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell` module and the third-party clients mined here all call `api.flow.microsoft.com` with the `Microsoft.ProcessSimple` provider paths. Neither surface supersedes the other in the corpus — they are two generations that are both live, and which one a caller gets depends on which client it is.

servers.description: The global Power Automate host. Regional prefixes such as `europe.` and `emea.` are used by some clients; none has been verified here.

post.description:
Sends several ProcessSimple requests in one call. It hangs off the host root with no resource provider, no environment and no `api-version` -- the sub-requests carry their own routes.

The admin centre uses it to read a flow and its sharing state together while monitoring an environment. Failure is reported per entry inside the body, so a batch can return successfully with every entry refused.

200.description: The sub-responses, in order. Each entry is either a result or an error; the outer status does not reflect the inner ones.

x-notes: The sub-request envelope's property name could not be recovered: the admin centre builds the body through a `batchOf` helper whose module is absent from the mined bundles. The entry shape (`method`, `url`) is witnessed; the name of the array holding them is not.

post.description:
Makes existing flows solution-aware by moving them into a solution.

**Read the resource provider again.** This route is under `Microsoft.Flow`, not `Microsoft.ProcessSimple`. It is the only one in this spec that is, and the difference is in the path rather than the host: the same host serves both namespaces. A client that builds flow URLs by templating the provider segment once will send this one to the wrong place.

parameters.description: The environment's name, which is its GUID. The literal alias `~default` selects the tenant default environment.

parameters.name: solutionId
parameters.description: The target solution's id.

parameters.name: api-version
parameters.description: The API version. Most shipped clients send `2016-11-01`; the owners route defaults to `2017-06-01`, and the admin centre pins `2016-11-01-beta` on the environment operations list. The admin flow list uses a `/v2/` path segment rather than a newer version.

get.description:
Environments visible to the caller on the Power Automate host. Distinct from the BAPI and Power Platform API environment lists: this one reports what the flow service knows, which can lag the platform.

The PowerShell admin module lists environments from three different hosts in one module -- BAPI, Power Apps and here -- which is worth knowing before treating any of them as authoritative.

get.description:
Pipeline deployment-stage runs for an environment: the history behind the admin centre's pipelines view, including approval state.

The query is Dataverse-shaped rather than ARM-shaped -- lowercase attribute names, `$select` of columns such as `approvalcomments` and `approvalstatus`, and filters over integer option-set values rather than strings. It reads like a Dataverse table surfaced through this host.

parameters.name: environmentName
parameters.description: The environment's name, which is its GUID. The literal alias `~default` selects the tenant default environment.

parameters.name: $select
parameters.description: Columns to return, lowercase Dataverse attribute names.

parameters.name: $filter
parameters.description: The admin centre composes up to three clauses: a fixed operation clause `((operation ne 200000201) or (operation eq 200000201 and operationstatus eq 200000003))`, an optional `starttime gt {iso8601}`, and an optional `operationstatus eq {code}`. The numbers are option-set values; what they name is not recoverable from the bundle.

parameters.name: $expand
parameters.description: The admin centre expands the stage.

x-notes: Two things separate this route from its neighbours and both are visible in the bundle rather than on the wire. It is built from a **different host constant** -- the admin centre calls it `flowV2` where every other route here uses `flow` -- so it may not be served by the host in this spec's `servers` block at all. And the reconstructed URL carries **no `api-version`**, where every sibling requires one.

Attaches a flow to a Power App.

The name is the interesting part: attaching a flow to an app is modelled as a **billing** link rather than an ownership or packaging one. The cmdlet that calls it is named after app context, and the route is named after who pays.

post.description:
Requests the tenant's Power Platform request (API call) consumption report.

It is tenant-wide and hangs directly off the resource provider: no environment segment, no admin scope, nothing between the provider and the verb.

The two-step shape matters more than the route. The POST does not return the report -- it returns a pre-signed download URL, which the client then fetches with no `Authorization` header at all. The report leaves through a second, unauthenticated request.

200.description: A pre-signed link to the report.

The follow-up download is the only fetch in the calling module that bypasses the API client entirely, because the raw bytes are wanted rather than a parsed object.

post.description:
Grants owner roles on a flow.

Two asymmetries are worth knowing before pairing this with anything. It exists **only** on the admin scope, while its natural counterpart -- revoking, through `modifyPermissions` -- is called on the user scope by the same module: granting an owner needs administrator reach, removing one does not.

And the segment is `modifyowners`, all lowercase, beside `modifyPermissions` on the same resource. A client that camel-cases by rule will miss it.

ApprovalList.description: Approvals or approval requests. Only `value` and, on a request, `properties.approval.title` are proven to be read by the PowerShell module; the rest of the item shape is unwitnessed and deliberately left open.

ApprovalResponse.description: The body a client sends to answer an approval. Three of its fields are literals the client fills in rather than choices: `properties.stage` is always `Basic`, `properties.status` is always `Committed` -- the client declares the response committed rather than letting the service decide -- and `properties.owner.type` is always `NotSpecified`.

response.description: The decision. This single field is the whole difference between approving and denying: both go to the same route with the same body.
response.x-enum-evidence: Both literals are in the module's source, one per cmdlet.

BatchRequest.description: A batch of sub-requests. The admin centre builds this through a `batchOf` helper whose own module is not in the mined bundles, so the name of the array property could not be recovered -- only the shape of the entries inside it.

BatchResponseItem.description: One sub-response. The admin centre reads two success fields and, on failure, a code and the inner HTTP status -- so a batch reports per-entry failure in the body rather than through the outer status.

workflowEntityId.description: The flow's Dataverse workflow row id, which is not the same identifier as the flow name used in the route.

code.x-enum-evidence: The set the admin centre's monitoring page branches on. Every one of them is a permission or lookup failure reported inside a 'successful' batch. Read from the bundle, not from a reply.

url.description: Host-relative, and addressed under the same resource provider as the rest of this spec.

BillingContextLink.description: The body shared by associate and dissociate. Identical in both directions, hardcoded literal included.

contextLinkType.description: A hardcoded literal in the client, not a choice: it sends `unifiedApp` and nothing else. Whether the service accepts any other value is unknown.
contextLinkType.x-enum-evidence: The only literal in the module's source; no other value appears in any client mined here.

contextLinkId.description: The Power App's name, which is its GUID.

ContentLink.description: A pointer to run content held outside this service. The `uri` addresses the underlying Logic Apps workflow host directly and carries its own pre-signed query string (`se`, `sp`, `sv`, `sig`), so it is fetched without this API's bearer token and expires on its own schedule. No example value is given here because a real one is a credential.

Environment.description:
An environment as the flow service reports it. Shape read from a client rather than from a reply: nothing in this spec has been observed on the wire, so this is what a working client expects to find, not what the service is known to send.

The fields here come from cli-microsoft365's own test fixtures for its environment commands; the PowerShell module reads a strict subset of the same names (`name`, `location`, `properties.displayName`, `properties.isDefault`, `properties.createdTime`, `properties.lastModifiedTime`), which is independent corroboration of that subset and silence about the rest.

name.description: The environment's id. The tenant default is named `Default-{tenantId}`.

createdBy.description: The principal that created the environment. A platform-created default environment reports the literal `SYSTEM` rather than a user.

isDefault.description: True for the one environment `~default` resolves to.

runtimeEndpoints.description: Per-service regional hosts for this environment, keyed by resource provider -- `microsoft.BusinessAppPlatform`, `microsoft.CommonDataModel`, `microsoft.PowerApps` and `microsoft.Flow`. The `microsoft.Flow` value is the regional form of this spec's own host, which is the closest thing here to an answer on whether the regional prefixes are real; it is still a field a client expects rather than one seen returned.

nextLink.description: Absent rather than null when there is no next page.

Flow.description:
A flow. Shape read from a client rather than from a reply: nothing in this spec has been observed on the wire, so this is what a working client expects to find, not what the service is known to send.

The enabled/disabled distinction is not a boolean on the wire: the PowerShell module derives it by comparing `properties.state` against the literal `Started`.

apiId.description: Always the Logic Flows connector: a flow is addressed here as a PowerApps API instance.

definition.description: The workflow definition, in the Logic Apps 2016-06-01 workflow definition language: `$schema`, `contentVersion`, `parameters` (including `$authentication` and `$connections`), `triggers` and `actions`.

state.description: `Started` means enabled. `Deleted` is what a soft-deleted flow reports in the admin list when `include=softDeletedFlows` is set.
state.x-enum-evidence: `Started` and `Deleted` appear in cli-microsoft365's fixtures; `Stopped` and `Suspended` are the values its and the PowerShell module's code branches on. None was seen returned by the service.

definitionSummary.description: Triggers and actions reduced to their types, so a list can be rendered without the whole definition.

isManaged.description: True for a flow that arrived in a managed solution.

machineDescriptionData.description: Desktop-flow machine metadata; empty for cloud flows.

flowOpenAiData.description: Whether the flow is treated as consequential when an AI agent invokes it, and whether an administrator has overridden that.

nextLink.description: Absent rather than null when there is no next page. The PowerShell module does not follow it at all and returns only the first page.

It is a distinct route from `permissions` and returns a richer principal: `email` and `displayName` as well as the id and type. Shape read from a client rather than from a reply: nothing in this spec has been observed on the wire, so this is what a working client expects to find, not what the service is known to send.

FlowPermission.description: One principal's access to one flow. Shape read from a client rather than from a reply: nothing in this spec has been observed on the wire, so this is what a working client expects to find, not what the service is known to send.

type.description: Note the leading slash: the client fixtures carry `/providers/Microsoft.ProcessSimple/environments/flows/permissions` here, which is not the unprefixed form the flow and run resources use.

roleName.x-enum-evidence: `Owner` and `CanEdit` appear in cli-microsoft365's fixtures; the admin centre hardcodes `CanEdit` when it grants co-ownership. `CanView` is the read role the same clients accept as input. None was seen returned by the service.

MigrateFlowsRequest.description: The flows to move into the solution.

flowsToMigrate.description: Flow names. An array even when there is one flow: the client wraps a single name rather than offering a scalar form.

ModifyOwnersRequest.description: The owner-grant body. Its `put` entries carry a richer principal than `modifyPermissions` does -- `email` and `displayName` as well as id and type.

ModifyPermissionsRequest.description: Grants and revokes in one body. `put` adds or updates roles, `delete` removes them by permission id. Clients send one or the other rather than both: cli-microsoft365 sends only `put` when adding an owner and only `delete` when removing one, and the PowerShell module sends only `delete`.

id.description: The full resource id of the permission to remove, not the principal's id.

RequestReport.description: Not the report. A pre-signed URL to it, in a PascalCase field that breaks with every other response shape in this spec.

DownloadLink.description: Fetched with no `Authorization` header -- the URL carries its own signature. The client reads the raw bytes rather than parsing them.

Run.description: One execution of a flow. Shape read from a client rather than from a reply: nothing in this spec has been observed on the wire, so this is what a working client expects to find, not what the service is known to send.

name.description: The run id, which is not a GUID: it is a long numeric string with a trailing scale-unit suffix.

status.x-enum-evidence: `Succeeded` appears in cli-microsoft365's fixtures; the rest are the values its commands and the PowerShell module branch on. None was seen returned by the service.

trigger.description: The firing that started the run, including links to its inputs and outputs.

name.description: The trigger's name from the flow definition.

nextLink.description: Absent rather than null when there is no next page.

TriggerList.description: A flow's triggers. The only field a client reads is `name`, which is what the resubmit route needs; nothing else about the item shape is witnessed.
